name: Tremella mushroom

lead: Tremella, or snow fungus, is an edible gelatinous fungus whose polysaccharide extracts are used in Asian skincare as a plant alternative to hyaluronic acid. People use it for skin that stays hydrated, looks plumper and shows softer fine lines.

The chain is water-holding: its polysaccharides are described as absorbing and holding water at the skin surface, so skin feels and looks more hydrated. A patent also reports inhibition of melanin formation, which is why some products pitch it for brightening. The sources found are encyclopedic descriptions and patents; clinical trials were not found.

paras: Used in essences, serums, creams and masks, applied to clean skin as a hydrating step under moisturiser. It is often combined with other humectants such as hyaluronic acid or glycerin. Users commonly report skin feeling more hydrated right after application, with a more lasting effect from consistent daily use.
No skincare safety data were found. The fungus itself is a long-established food in Chinese cuisine, and topical products carry standard irritation precautions.

angle.text: Tremella polysaccharides are used in Asian skincare as a plant-based alternative to hyaluronic acid, holding water at the skin surface so skin looks plumper and fine lines look softer. A patent also describes it reducing melanin formation for a brighter tone.

lead: Tremella fuciformis, known as snow fungus or silver ear, is an edible, gelatinous white fungus whose polysaccharide extracts are used in Asian skincare as moisturisers and for anti-wrinkle and brightening effects. People use tremella-based products, and eat the fungus in soups and desserts, for skin that looks hydrated and plump.[1]

Wikipedia reports that extracts appear in beauty products in China, Korea and Japan and are said to increase moisture retention in the skin, possibly reduce wrinkles and raise superoxide dismutase, an antioxidant enzyme; it presents these as reported claims.[1] A US patent describes a tremella polysaccharide for skin care with moisturising and melanin-formation-inhibiting effects.[2]

A human study of a snow mushroom hand gel in 20 volunteers found it moisturised the skin significantly better than placebo at all time points up to 180 minutes and was non-irritating.[3] A 2025 review summarises tremella polysaccharide research, mostly on immune, antioxidant and metabolic activities.[4]
infobox: Snow fungus, silver ear, white jelly mushroom
China, since at least the 19th century[1]

paras: The fungus forms white, frond-like fruit bodies up to about 7 cm across and grows as a parasitic yeast on other fungi on dead broadleaf wood. Berkeley described it in 1856 from Brazilian collections.[1] It has been cultivated in China since at least the 19th century, and a modern dual-culture method with its host fungus is used; estimated Chinese output in 1997 was 130,000 tonnes.[1]

Names include yin'er (silver ear), xue'er (snow ear) and bai mu'er (white wood ear) in Mandarin, shiro kikurage in Japanese, and ngan nhi in Vietnamese. Berkeley's 1856 description was based on specimens collected in Brazil by Richard Spruce, and a 1939 species named Nakaiomyces nipponicus was later shown to be T. fuciformis parasitised by an ascomycete and is now a synonym.[1] Early Chinese cultivation was haphazard, using treated wooden poles; inoculating poles with spores or mycelium improved yields, and modern commercial production inoculates a sawdust mix with both Tremella and its host fungus Annulohypoxylon archeri.[1]
Traditionally it is used in sweet soups and desserts such as the Cantonese dessert soup luk mei and, in traditional Chinese medicine, is valued for nourishing the lungs and increasing yin.[1]

In cosmetics, extracts are reported to retain moisture, reduce wrinkles and raise superoxide dismutase levels; Wikipedia presents these as reported claims.[1] A 2006 US patent describes a tremella polysaccharide for skin care with moisturizing and melanin-formation-inhibiting effects.[2] A 2008 patent describes use for intestinal disorders.[5]

Culinary use centres on its gelatinous texture rather than its flavour. It is commonly cooked with jujubes and dried longans in luk mei dessert soup, appears in drinks and ice cream, and in Vietnamese cuisine is used in che sweet drinks and desserts; lower cultivation costs have brought it into some savoury dishes.[1] Wikipedia says extracts in China, Korea and Japan are reported to smooth fine lines and have anti-inflammatory uses.[1]

A 2021 Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology study formulated an alcohol-based hand gel with 10 percent snow mushroom extract and tested it in 20 Thai volunteers. The gel moisturised the skin significantly better than placebo at all intervals through 180 minutes, caused no irritation and had antiseptic efficacy comparable with the placebo gel.[3]

A 2023 randomized trial of a fish roe, snow fungus and yeast supplement examined cognitive function rather than skin.[6] No studies found of tremella skincare on facial wrinkles or pigmentation. A 2025 review covers extraction, structure and bioactivities of tremella polysaccharides, including immunomodulatory, antioxidant, anti-hyperglycemic and anti-hyperlipidemia effects.[4]

As a food, snow fungus is long established. Food-safety research on it concerns contaminants rather than skin effects. A 2020 assessment of 91 snow fungus samples from Fujian Province, China, found 13 pesticides, with 65.9% of samples containing at least one residue; the study reported a very low chronic hazard quotient for adults and young children.[7] A 2026 paper on detecting bongkrekic acid, a respiratory toxin produced by Pseudomonas cocovenenans found in spoiled fermented rice and wheat products, snow fungus and black fungus, describes rapid screening methods to prevent food poisoning.[8] No skincare safety data beyond the hand gel study were found.

A 2025 review of Tremella fuciformis polysaccharides summarises work on extraction, purification and structure, along with reported microbial-homeostasis, immunomodulatory, antioxidant, anti-hyperglycemic and anti-hyperlipidemia activities, and describes the polysaccharides as candidates for functional foods and therapeutic development.[4] A 2026 chromatographic study profiled more than 500 volatile and semi-volatile compounds across six edible mushrooms including snow fungus.[9] In the 2023 cognition trial, 64 participants took a fish roe, snow fungus and yeast beverage or placebo for 8 weeks, and the formula group showed faster responses and more memory cards on tests.[6]
